newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Greens to talk economics but Bosnia looms.
newsitem.headline: German Greens to talk economics but Bosnia looms.

text.p: Members of Germany's opposition Greens begin a party congress on Friday, hoping to portray themselves as a responsible future party of government but with a divisive debate looming over Bosnia.

The environmentalist party wants to use the conference, due to open on Friday evening in the eastern city of Suhl, to show how far it has come from its roots in the peace movement and radical anti-capitalist student protests of the 1960s and 1970s.

"Anyone who wants to rule Germany after 1998 (when the next general elections are due) has to make reality the basis of their reforms," Joschka Fischer, the party's pragmatic co-leader in parliament, told the Suedeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

The Greens, the third-largest party in parliament, will devote much of the conference to economic policy to convince voters they are ready to help topple Chancellor Helmut Kohl and form a coalition with main opposition Social Democrats.
But the thorny issue of using violence to bring peace to war zones looks set to crop up again after leading Greens went on a fact-finding trip to Bosnia last month.
Hoping to avoid a repeat of a row at last year's conference, organisers have not allocated time for a debate on the subject.

But ordinary members will get a chance to vote on which motions should be debated during the three-day congress. The grassroots, often more pacifist and idealistic than leading figures, could well decide to force a debate on Bosnia.
Pragmatists such as Fischer returned from the fact-finding trip strengthened in their conviction that German troops should take part in the next international peace mission in Bosnia.
"When it comes to foreign policy, the Greens are still arguing about questions of peace-keeping but really it's more about face-keeping for the left wing," Fischer said.

But the likes of party co-leader Juergen Trittin are still holding fast to the Greens' pacifist past and insist Kohl's government is hijacking the humanitarian need in Bosnia to throw off Germany's post-war military shackles.

A debate on Bosnia could serve as a litmus test not only of how far the Greens have grown from their roots but also of how much anti-militarism, once popular among large sections of post-war German society, still has a role to play in the 1990s.

At last year's conference in Bremen, the Greens voted to reject the use of military intervention to resolve armed conflicts. The party's deputies split when it came to a parliamentary vote on sending German troops to Bosnia.

Many leading figures in the party say they would rather not have the debate this year at all, preferring to concentrate on economic policy proposals, such as a radical plan to cut the basic rate of income tax by almost six points to 20 percent.
